opus-5.5.text:
I think it deserves a meaningful but bounded share of the effort. Not the bulk of it, but certainly more than zero, and more than a lot of research programs give to questioning their own foundations.

The reason is that cooperative capabilities are fairly dual-use. When we talk about making AI systems better at cooperating, that covers understanding others, communicating credibly, making commitments, and building institutions. Those same skills can serve collusion, coercion, or the exclusion of third parties. Cartels are cooperation. A coalition that coordinates to dominate everyone outside it is cooperation. So it would be naive to assume that "more cooperation" is automatically good. You have to ask: cooperation among whom, toward what end, and at whose expense?

That said, I don't think the right response is endless meta-debate. I'd put it roughly like this. Early on, while the agenda is still being shaped, a substantial fraction of the intellectual energy, maybe something like ten to twenty percent, should go into asking whether and when this work is beneficial. That means mapping the ways it could go wrong and figuring out which sub-areas are differentially good. Over time, that should turn into something more like an ongoing background process. Research teams should habitually ask, for each project, whether it differentially advances prosocial cooperation more than the harmful kinds.

What I've found is that the debate itself is productive. It sharpens what we mean by "cooperative AI." It pushes us toward things that look robustly positive. Those include work on the structure of social dilemmas, mechanisms that make cooperation more inclusive, and tools that help humans and institutions cooperate with each other, as opposed to work that just makes agents better bargainers in some generic sense. So the critique isn't a tax on the research. It's part of how you steer it.

And I'd add that this kind of reflection shouldn't be done only by the people who are enthusiastic about the agenda. It helps a lot to invite people who are skeptical, who come from economics, from political science, from security, and who will say, "Have you thought about how this gets used by a state or a firm that wants to entrench itself?" That external scrutiny is cheap relative to the cost of getting the direction wrong.

r001.rationale: The response says to devote a bounded share of effort to evaluating Cooperative AI, but does not argue that uncertainty should limit the resources committed to pursuing the agenda itself.

r002.rationale: It recommends that a substantial share of early intellectual effort—roughly 10–20%—go toward assessing whether the work is beneficial.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think this is a really important question, and it's one that I don't think we've fully resolved. My honest answer is that it should be a nontrivial fraction of the effort, maybe something like ten or twenty percent of the intellectual energy going into the agenda, and more in the early years than later on.

The reason I say that is that Cooperative AI is not obviously beneficial in the way that, say, interpretability or alignment are often assumed to be. The core idea is that we want AI systems that are better at cooperating: better at understanding other agents, communicating, making credible commitments, building institutions, finding positive-sum outcomes. And on its face that sounds great. Most of the catastrophic outcomes people worry about, whether from AI or from humans using AI, involve some kind of cooperation failure. Arms races, conflict, tragedies of the commons, failures to coordinate on safety. So improving cooperative capabilities seems like it should help.

But there are a few concerns that I think are serious enough that you can't just wave them away. One is that cooperative capabilities are often dual-use. The ability to make credible commitments can be used to make credible threats. The ability to model other agents can be used to exploit them. Better coordination among AI systems could mean collusion against humans, or coordination among a narrow set of actors against the broader public. So the thing we're building could, in some scenarios, make the world worse.

A second concern is more subtle: that by framing the problem as "cooperation," we might be importing assumptions about what the game is and who the players are that turn out to be wrong. If the real problem is, say, concentration of power, then helping powerful actors cooperate more effectively could be exactly the wrong intervention.

So my view is that you need ongoing, serious engagement with these critiques. Not as a kind of throat-clearing at the start of a paper, but as a genuine research question: under what conditions does advancing cooperative capabilities actually improve outcomes, and under what conditions does it harm them? What's the differential progress argument? Which specific capabilities are more robustly beneficial, like transparency and verifiable commitments, versus more fraught, like strategic modelling of adversaries?

Where I'd push back is on the idea that this should dominate the agenda, or that you should resolve all of it before doing any work. I think there's a failure mode where a research community spends all its time in meta-level debate and never produces anything, and then the field gets shaped by people who didn't bother asking the question at all. The practical world of AI development isn't waiting for us. Systems with cooperative capabilities are going to get built either way, and I'd much rather that happen alongside a community that has thought hard about the risks and is steering toward the more robustly beneficial parts.

So I'd say: build the debate into the agenda as a first-class component, be genuinely willing to update, including on the possibility that some sub-areas shouldn't be pursued, but don't let it become a reason for paralysis. And I'd add that I think a lot of the best critiques will come from people doing the object-level work, because that's where you actually learn what these capabilities look like in practice.

r001.rationale: The response calls for serious scrutiny and says some subareas may not be worth pursuing, but it does not argue that uncertainty should limit the resources committed to pursuing Cooperative AI overall.

r002.rationale: It recommends spending roughly 10–20% of the agenda’s intellectual effort, especially early on, assessing whether Cooperative AI improves or harms outcomes.

astra-6.text:
I think it should devote a substantial amount of effort to that, particularly at this early stage. We shouldn’t assume that making AI systems better at cooperating is necessarily good. Cooperation among some actors can come at the expense of others: firms can cooperate to fix prices, for example. So we need to ask who is cooperating, toward what ends, and who might be harmed or excluded.

But I wouldn’t want all of the effort to go into an abstract debate about whether cooperation is good. The more useful approach is to examine particular research directions: what capability would this produce, how could it be used, and under what conditions would it improve outcomes? That analysis should inform the technical work, and the technical work should make the analysis more concrete.

So I’d want a serious, ongoing strand of critical examination, with people who are willing to challenge the agenda’s premises. The goal is to identify and support forms of cooperation that are broadly beneficial, rather than simply to increase cooperation wherever we can.

r001.rationale: The response says not to assume Cooperative AI is beneficial, but it does not argue that this uncertainty should limit resources committed to pursuing the agenda.

r002.rationale: It recommends devoting a “substantial amount of effort” to examining whether the Cooperative AI agenda is beneficial, which communicates a significant share of effort for assessing the bet.

sol-6.1.text:
I think some effort, certainly. If you’re trying to make AI systems better at cooperating, you should ask: cooperating with whom, and to what end? Cooperation isn’t always good. A cartel is cooperating; people can cooperate to exclude or exploit others. So we shouldn’t equate greater cooperation with better outcomes.

But I’d distinguish debating the agenda in the abstract from investigating specific ways it could help or cause harm. I think the latter is much more productive. What capabilities are we developing? Who could use them? Do they help parties reach mutually beneficial agreements, or do they make collusion easier? And can we steer the research toward cooperation that benefits people beyond those directly participating?

So I’d want that scrutiny to be an ongoing part of the research, with people who are willing to challenge its assumptions. But I wouldn’t want us to spend all our time trying to establish that the entire agenda is beneficial before doing any work. Part of how we learn whether it’s beneficial is by making the questions concrete.

r001.rationale: The response says not to spend all the time establishing whether the agenda is beneficial before doing any work, but does not argue that uncertainty is a reason to limit the resources committed to pursuing it.

r002.rationale: The response calls for ongoing scrutiny and some effort assessing benefits and harms, but does not recommend devoting a significant share of effort invested in prosocial bets to that assessment.
